title: Why is "don't over-engineer" a core LLD skill (avoid forcing patterns, avoid a God class, start simple and refactor), and how do you answer the common follow-up "how would you extend this?" using the Open/Closed Principle (add a new class, not modify existing code)?
shortTitle: Why "don't over-engineer" is a core LLD skill, and answering "how would you extend this?" with the Open/Closed Principle

s1_definition.profdef: Not over-engineering is the discipline of building the simplest design that correctly satisfies the current requirements, avoiding speculative abstractions, forced patterns, and sprawling God classes, and refactoring toward more structure only when a real need appears. It is a core low-level design skill because interviewers judge not just whether you know patterns, but whether you know when not to use them. The natural follow-up, "how would you extend this," is answered with the Open/Closed Principle: a good design lets you add a new class to introduce new behaviour without modifying existing, tested code.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose National Bank of India asks you to design a system that today supports exactly one kind of fee. Over-engineering is building a configurable rule engine, a plugin framework, and a message bus for that single fee — you have built a mansion when a room was asked for. The skilled move is to build the simple room cleanly and leave an obvious doorway for a future room. Then when the interviewer asks, "what if we add a second fee type next year?" you answer calmly: because I kept the fee behaviour behind a small interface, I just add one new class for the new fee, and I never touch the existing fee code. You extend by adding, not by editing — that is the Open/Closed Principle, and it is the reward for not over-engineering while still designing cleanly.
s1_definition.oneliner: Build the simplest correct design and refactor when needed, then extend by adding a new class rather than modifying existing code, which is the Open/Closed Principle.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Not over-engineering is the discipline of building the simplest design that correctly satisfies the current requirements, avoiding speculative abstractions, forced patterns, and sprawling God classes, and refactoring toward more structure only when a real need appears. It is a core low-level design skill because interviewers judge not just whether you know patterns, but whether you know when not to use them. The natural follow-up, "how would you extend this," is answered with the Open/Closed Principle: a good design lets you add a new class to introduce new behaviour without modifying existing, tested code.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose National Bank of India asks you to design a system that today supports exactly one kind of fee. Over-engineering is building a configurable rule engine, a plugin framework, and a message bus for that single fee — you have built a mansion when a room was asked for. The skilled move is to build the simple room cleanly and leave an obvious doorway for a future room. Then when the interviewer asks, "what if we add a second fee type next year?" you answer calmly: because I kept the fee behaviour behind a small interface, I just add one new class for the new fee, and I never touch the existing fee code. You extend by adding, not by editing — that is the Open/Closed Principle, and it is the reward for not over-engineering while still designing cleanly.

**One line to remember:** Build the simplest correct design and refactor when needed, then extend by adding a new class rather than modifying existing code, which is the Open/Closed Principle.

sections.s2_technical:
Over-engineering is adding complexity the problem does not justify. It shows up as **forced patterns** — using a Strategy, Factory, or Observer where a plain method would do; as a **God class** — one class that accumulates many responsibilities and becomes impossible to change safely; as **speculative generality** — building for imagined future requirements that may never arrive; and as **premature abstraction** — extracting interfaces and layers before there is any real variation. Each of these adds files, indirection, and cognitive load, making the code harder to read and change, which is the opposite of what good design is for.

Why is avoiding it a **core low-level design skill**? Because in an LLD interview, piling on patterns signals immaturity, not expertise. Senior engineers know that every abstraction has a cost, and that the simplest design that meets the requirements is usually the most maintainable. The judgment of when a pattern earns its place — and when it does not — is exactly what distinguishes a strong candidate. The disciplined approach is to **start simple and refactor**: write the cohesive, straightforward model first, keep responsibilities clear, and introduce a pattern precisely when a real pressure appears, such as a second variant, a growing switch statement, or a hard-to-test dependency. This also connects to KISS, keep it simple, and YAGNI, you are not going to need it.

Avoiding a **God class** deserves its own emphasis. A God class violates the Single Responsibility Principle by doing many unrelated things, so it changes for many reasons, is hard to test, and becomes a merge-conflict magnet. The fix is to split responsibilities into focused classes, each with one job, which keeps the design cohesive and changeable.

Now the critical part: **answering "how would you extend this?" with the Open/Closed Principle.** The Open/Closed Principle says software should be open for extension but closed for modification. In practice this means you design so that new behaviour is added by writing a new class that plugs into an existing abstraction, rather than by editing existing, working code. When the interviewer asks how you would add a new vehicle type, a new payment method, a new fee rule, or a new notification channel, the ideal answer is: "I would add a new class that implements the existing interface, and register it — I would not modify the existing classes at all." For example, if parking fees are computed through a `FeeStrategy` interface, adding an electric-vehicle fee is a new `EvFeeStrategy` class; the parking lot and the other strategies are untouched. This is powerful because untouched code does not need re-testing and cannot regress, which is why the Open/Closed Principle reduces risk in a banking system where a regression can mean financial loss.

The subtle wisdom is balancing these two ideas, because they can seem to pull in opposite directions. Not over-engineering says do not add abstractions on speculation; the Open/Closed Principle seems to want abstractions ready for extension. The resolution is that you do not pre-build abstractions for every imagined axis of change. You keep the design simple, but you identify the one or two axes where change is genuinely likely — for a bank, new fee types or new account products are likely, new database vendors usually are not — and you place a seam, a small interface, only along those likely axes. So your design is simple today yet open along the dimensions that really will change. When the interviewer probes extension on an axis you anticipated, you add a class; if they probe an unlikely axis, you honestly say you would refactor to introduce a seam at that point, because designing for every possible future is itself over-engineering.

A senior nuance: the best candidates demonstrate both halves in one breath — "here is the simplest model that meets today's requirements, and because new fee types are a likely change, I put the fee behind a small strategy interface, so adding one later is a new class, not an edit." That shows you avoid over-engineering while still designing for the Open/Closed Principle where it counts.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India needs to send a transaction alert. Today there is exactly one channel: SMS. A colleague wanted to build a full plugin framework with dynamic class loading, a configuration-driven channel registry, and an event bus, for a single SMS channel. That is over-engineering — huge machinery for one channel, a God-class registry, and speculative generality. The skilled approach is a simple design with one small seam along the axis that genuinely will change, which is the notification channel, because the bank is very likely to add email and push later.

Problem 2 — When the interviewer asks "how would you add email and push notifications?", we want to answer with the Open/Closed Principle: add a new class implementing the existing channel interface, register it, and touch no existing channel code. We will actually demonstrate this by adding a second channel as a new class.

In the mini-project we will build a `NotificationService` that sends alerts through a small `NotificationChannel` interface, with an initial `SmsChannel`. The service is thin and holds a list of channels. We will send Rajesh a transaction alert via SMS. Then, to show Open/Closed extension, we will add an `EmailChannel` as a brand-new class and register it, without modifying the service or the SMS channel, and send Priya an alert through both channels. We will keep everything deliberately simple — no plugin framework, no God class — to show not-over-engineering and clean extensibility together.

The code contains: a `NotificationChannel` interface; an `SmsChannel`; a thin `NotificationService`; and then an `EmailChannel` added as a new class to demonstrate extension by addition.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transaction alert for Rajesh, then after extension an alert for Priya.

Step 1: We build a `NotificationService` and register a single `SmsChannel`. We deliberately did not build a plugin framework, a configuration-driven registry, or an event bus, because the requirement is one channel. The only structure we added is a small `NotificationChannel` interface, placed along the one axis genuinely likely to change — the channel.

Step 2: We call `notifyCustomer` for Rajesh. The service loops over its channels, which currently is just the SMS channel, and delegates the send. The SMS channel logs the alert. The design is as simple as it can be while meeting the requirement.

Step 3: The extension requirement arrives, mirroring the interviewer's "how would you extend this?" We add an `EmailChannel` as a brand-new class. Critically, we do not edit the `NotificationService` or the `SmsChannel` at all. The new class implements the existing interface.

Step 4: We register the email channel and call `notifyCustomer` for Priya. The service loops over both channels and sends through SMS and email. The `notifyCustomer` method itself never changed — it was closed for modification but the system was open for extension by adding a class.

Step 5: Because the existing SMS channel and the service were untouched, they do not need re-testing and cannot regress. This is the risk-reduction benefit of the Open/Closed Principle, and it was only possible because we placed one seam along the right axis rather than over-engineering many speculative ones.

```
2026-10-26 10:55:00 [INFO] === Today: single SMS channel (simplest correct design) ===
2026-10-26 10:55:00 [INFO] [SMS] to Rajesh: Rs.50000 debited from SAV2001
2026-10-26 10:55:00 [INFO] === Extension via Open/Closed: add EmailChannel (new class) ===
2026-10-26 10:55:00 [INFO] [SMS] to Priya: Rs.75000 credited to CUR3001
2026-10-26 10:55:00 [INFO] [EMAIL] to Priya: Rs.75000 credited to CUR3001
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Not over-engineering is the discipline of building the simplest design that correctly meets today's requirements, and it is a core low-level design skill because interviewers judge whether I know when not to use a pattern just as much as whether I know the patterns. Over-engineering shows up as forced patterns where a plain method would do, as a God class that does too many things and changes for too many reasons, as speculative generality built for an imagined future, and as premature abstraction introduced before any real variation exists. Each of these adds indirection and cognitive load and makes the code harder to change, which is the opposite of what design is for.

So my approach is to start simple and refactor. I write the cohesive, straightforward model first, keep each class to a single responsibility so I avoid a God class, and introduce a pattern only when a real pressure appears, such as a second variant, a growing switch statement, or a hard-to-test dependency. This is KISS and YAGNI applied to design.

The common follow-up is how would you extend this, and I answer it with the Open/Closed Principle, which says software should be open for extension but closed for modification. In practice that means new behaviour is added by writing a new class that plugs into an existing abstraction, not by editing existing, working code. So when asked how I would add a new payment method, vehicle type, fee rule, or notification channel, my answer is that I add a new class implementing the existing interface and register it, and I touch none of the existing classes. That reduces risk, because untouched code cannot regress and does not need re-testing, which matters enormously in a bank.

The judgment that ties it together is balancing these two ideas, because not over-engineering says do not add speculative abstractions, while Open/Closed wants seams ready for extension. I resolve it by not pre-building abstractions for every possible future, but identifying the one or two axes where change is genuinely likely — for a bank, new fee types or account products are likely, new database vendors usually are not — and placing a small interface only along those likely axes. In my notification project I kept the service thin with a single SMS channel and placed one seam, a channel interface, because new channels were clearly coming. When email and push were later needed, each was a new class with zero edits to the existing code. That is how I demonstrate both halves at once: the simplest design that meets today's needs, open for extension exactly where change will really happen.

keyPoints: S: Single Responsibility — one class, one reason to change
O: Open/Closed — open for extension, closed for modification
L: Liskov Substitution — subtypes must be substitutable for base types
I: Interface Segregation — many specific interfaces over one general
D: Dependency Inversion — depend on abstractions, not concrete classes
